Designing Breakwaters

A breakwater protects a harbour by taking the force of the waves before they reach the boats, and engineers choose its shape from the height of the storms it has to survive and the depth of the water in front of it.

Rubble mound breakwaters are built from layers of stone, with the largest blocks on the outside, so that the waves lose their energy in the gaps between the stones instead of breaking against a wall.

Vertical breakwaters use a concrete wall instead, which takes less space but reflects the waves back to the sea, so they are built where the water is deep enough that the reflected waves do no harm.

Many harbours combine both designs, with a rubble mound at the base and a concrete crown on top, which keeps the structure low and still stops the waves from washing over it during storms.
